title: Carlo Rovelli’s romantic pragmatism
gist: A profile of physicist Carlo Rovelli, who has published two 2026 books—one a furious history of nuclear weapons (85 Seconds to Midnight), the other a serene relational philosophy (On the Equality of All Things)—that make the same argument: fear and the failure to think relationally, rather than physics itself, drive nations toward catastrophe.

insights.claim: Rovelli’s two 2026 books—85 Seconds to Midnight on nuclear weapons and On the Equality of All Things on relational philosophy—advance the same underlying thesis despite opposite tones.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
entities: On the Equality of All Things
insights.so_what: The unifying claim—that relational thinking is a survival skill for geopolitics—is the interpretive key to both works.

insights.claim: 85 Seconds to Midnight is named for the current, unprecedented setting of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists’ Doomsday Clock, which scientists moved closer to midnight in January.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Anchors the nuclear-risk thesis to a widely tracked risk indicator at an all-time-worst reading.

insights.claim: Rovelli argues the Manhattan Project was a colossal investment premised on the false belief that Hitler was closing in on a super-bomb, when Germany’s physicists had told the Nazis a bomb could not be built before the war’s end.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Reframes the founding rationale of the nuclear age as an intelligence failure—useful lens for reading today’s threat inflation.
insights.quote: There was a profound misunderstanding in the UK and US about what was actually happening in Germany

insights.claim: Rovelli contends Truman used the bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki—after Germany’s surrender and amid Japanese signals toward a negotiated end—to keep the Soviets out of Tokyo and announce US dominance.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Casts the bombings as a demonstration of power rather than military necessity—a revisionist frame with political charge.
insights.quote: the scream of the gorilla beating its chest and telling the forest that it is the strongest

insights.claim: Rovelli reads the Korean War as born of two mirror-image intelligence failures—Moscow sure the US wouldn’t defend the south, Washington sure China wouldn’t defend the north—that cost millions of lives.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Illustrates the recurring pattern of catastrophic miscalculation from failing to model the adversary’s beliefs.
insights.locator: From there, the ledger of errors

insights.claim: Rovelli argues that for small countries the bomb is 'life insurance'—Libya gave up its programme and was bombed into chaos while North Korea kept its and remains untouched—while for great powers it is an instrument of domination.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A proliferation incentive model that predicts why disarmament pledges are unreliable—relevant to nonproliferation risk.
insights.locator: Libya gave up its nuclear programme

insights.claim: Rovelli stresses that today’s warheads are hundreds of times more powerful than those dropped on Japan and number in the many thousands, making the nuclear problem one of the present, not the past.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Reframes nuclear risk as a live, escalating tail hazard rather than a Cold War relic.
insights.quote: The problem of atomic bombs is not the past; it’s the present
insights.locator: And what mistakes will happen in future?

insights.claim: Rovelli warns that because American bombs are stationed in England and northern Italy, those regions would be among the first destroyed in a nuclear exchange—dying 'first, to save the Americans.'
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Highlights the co-location risk that host countries of US weapons carry in any escalation.
insights.locator: He gestures, loosely, at the city around us

insights.claim: Rovelli holds that most aggression springs from fear, which is irrational because it is reciprocal—each side’s fear feeds the other’s aggression.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A causal model of escalation spirals applicable to arms races and confrontation dynamics.
insights.quote: So much of the worst aggressivity comes from fear
insights.locator: And the moral of it all?

insights.claim: Rovelli’s philosophy holds that the world is made not of things but of relations—entities, including people, are constituted entirely by their interactions and connections.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
entities: On the Equality of All Things
insights.so_what: The relational ontology is the mental model he extends from quantum physics to geopolitics.
insights.quote: We are relations, in that sense.
insights.locator: When I ask him to summarise

insights.claim: Rovelli insists relationalism does not collapse into relativism, using the sunset as an example: it exists as the name of what happens each evening even though Copernicus showed the sun does not sink.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Guards the worldview against the ‘anything goes’ critique—both everyday and scientific images can be true and incomplete.
insights.locator: Rovelli’s running example is the sunset

insights.claim: Rovelli argues that thinking in terms of countries and their fixed identities and interests positions us badly, and that the missing step in press, politics and decision-making is asking how the enemy sees reality.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A prescriptive frame for conflict analysis: model the adversary’s perspective or risk suicidal confrontation.
insights.quote: If there’s a problem, we should heal the network.
insights.locator: If reality is relational, he emphasises

insights.claim: While calling Russia’s invasion of Ukraine criminal, illegal and an obvious mistake, Rovelli urges reckoning with how it looks from Moscow and with the West’s own record of attacking other countries since 1945.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: The perspective-taking stance that draws accusations of appeasement—signals the fault line in his public reception.
insights.locator: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, he is careful

insights.claim: Rovelli openly distinguishes three levels in his nuclear history—researched facts, a chosen narrative that others could construct differently, and an intended point—conceding the book is both history and polemic.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A candid account of how argumentative nonfiction is constructed—useful for weighting its claims.
insights.quote: History is not objective. You can choose this fact and that fact

insights.claim: Rovelli’s activism—a 2023 May Day speech attacking Italy’s defence minister and open letters against European rearmament—briefly got him disinvited from the 2024 Frankfurt Book Fair until an outcry reversed it.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Shows the reputational stakes and institutional friction around anti-rearmament positions in Europe.

insights.claim: Rovelli argues theoretical physics has been sterile for decades because a superficial reading of Popper and Kuhn pushed it to fish for exotic theories rather than work patiently outward from established knowledge.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A working scientist’s critique of his own field’s research strategy—relevant to how fundamental science allocates effort.
